# Part X: Ecosystem and Economics {#part-ecosystem .unnumbered}

> "A wealth of information creates a poverty of attention."
>
> Herbert A. Simon, ["Designing Organizations for an Information-Rich World"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attention_economy)

The previous parts have shown how models are trained, served, composed,
measured, and constrained. Part X asks who can afford to do those things, who
packages them for everyone else, and how the prices feed back into design. The
ecosystem is not scenery around the technical stack. It is one of the forces that
decides which parts of the stack become common practice.

A model release is an economic object as much as a technical one, and
@sec-model-landscape reads it on both axes: weights or API, open source AI or
open weights, capability or efficiency, license or lock-in. @sec-tooling-ecosystem
then follows the standards and layers that grew around model calls, tools, agents,
gateways, sandboxes, observability, and authorization. Beneath both lies a cost
structure, which @sec-economics lays out: training and inference run on different
clocks, and market prices move as the field matures.

The second half of the part turns from artifacts to markets. @sec-market-structure
maps the AI value chain from silicon and cloud to model APIs, applications, and
data. Capability does not automatically become productivity, and
@sec-adoption-productivity asks when it does so in a real workflow rather than a
demo. @sec-data-rights-economics treats data as a rights-bearing supply chain,
where provenance, consent, documentation, and compliance determine whether a
corpus can become a product input.

This part shifts attention away from any single leaderboard point and toward the
terms under which capability is made available. A model can be strong and still
unavailable, cheap and still costly to operate, open and still hard to use
responsibly. Economics is where those differences become part of the
architecture.
